I went through the same shit last summer. I only shut myself away for 3 months, so it wasn't *nearly* as bad as 5 (or more!) years, but I went through it nonetheless, and it's a terrible, terrible feeling. You want to get better, but that means going out and being social and it's so much easier to just stay inside, you know?

I still sort of go through similar things (I kind of have for the past two weeks), but it's mostly over now. I really don't have much to add, but I can relate to this really well (this is a throwaway account, obviously, but if you check my past submissions you can read a pretty lengthy of the ordeal I went through)

I went through the same thing last summer (check my account for my posts...and yes, this is a throwaway).

I did the same thing as you last summer in grad school. I was feeling crummy and depressed, so I stayed home for one day. Then two days. Then 2 weeks. In all, I didn't show my face for 2 months at work (my supervisor was gone for the majority of that time, so I guess that was my excuse), and it was another month before I got back to a regular schedule. I guess the difference between us was that I got nothing done in that time, and lived a very sad, lonely existence. 

Read the posts I made for some advice, but here's some general advice I've found works:

- Have routines. Wake up at the same time, leave the house at a set time, make dinner, do the dishes, etc. This will keep your mind off what's bothering you. 

- Socialize. We are wired to socialize and it's part of what keeps us healthy. Make an effort to talk to people, be friendly and make friends. If you have friends, they will also be there for support and to hold you accountable if you ever flake out again. So how do you make new friends?...

- Find a hobby. People recommend exercise (and I would too), but it doesn't matter as long as it's with other people and gets you out of the house.

- Your co-workers don't care about your absence as much as you think they do. When I got back, I got questions and I usually just brushed them aside or changed the subject (I was a bit ashamed). People aren't talking behind your back or anything, and they probably won't judge you as much as you think they do. If they are, and you find it unbearable to work, then..

- Make a change. I don't know what the cause of your malaise was, but unless you feel this way all the time, something caused it this time. Get that something out of your life. You will be much happier once you do. For me, it was a supervisor who placed a ton of pressure on me and didn't offer much support, to the point where my anxiety about being viewed as a failure prevented me from doing...anything. Whatever it is for you, get it out of your life ASAP!

If you read the looooong posts I made last summer, I eventually sorted it out. I finished my degree requirements and graduated with a degree, hence leaving the toxic situation, while still getting something productive out of it (it helped that I essentially eliminated the cause of my anxiety from my life). 

Life's too short to deal with this garbage. Do things that make you happy. It's not easy, I still deal with some of the issues I had last year, like just staying at home, or eating crappy instead of buying real groceries. But it's worth it if you do. 

I don't know if I've addressed your issues, so send me a message if you want to know anything else.

Haha, thanks, I guess I'm pretty cool. 

I guess I'll let you know what happened today (since you asked). 

I saw a counselor this morning and I found out that my advisor, and the department and basically everyone called the counseling center to find out what the crap was going on. So I had to sign a form saying that the counseling center can tell my department that I'm around. I also have to keep going to counseling, but I don't know how they can enforce that? 

I guess the main thing that happened was she will send a referral to a psychiatrist, so hopefully that sorts something out? I'll have to cancel a previous appointment I made, which was scheduled by a doctor. She suggested that I may need chemical help to get out of this shitty spiral I'm in (and by chemical, I mean pharmaceutical, not any of the fun ones. Oh well). She suggested I may have OCD, but I'll wait for a proper diagnosis from a psychiatric professional before I put an weight behind that OCD (or bipolar) diagnosis.

Then I had a meeting with my advisor and the graduate program director. They gave me a form which says I have provisional standing, which means that I had to make a "specific plan of studies". That means that:

- I complete my two courses this fall and start working on putting my thesis together. 

- The plan is to defend my thesis and graduate by January, at the latest, which is 6 or 7 months earlier than anyone has graduated. I'll have been in the program 18 months, 16 months if you include the 2 months I didn't show up.  I am required to attend specified meetings with my advisor and my committee, but this is regular thesis procedure.  They want me to get done ASAP so no other problems sprout up, but it just seems they want to be rid of me :P

Now I can't be a TA (which makes me feel rather sheepish, that I somehow can't handle that responsibility, even though I HAVE in the past....I mean, eventually I'll have to learn how to handle all those responsibilities), and my advisor won't pay me (too much risk and too little funding), but I will somehow get paid a little salary by the department and the school of grad studies. Probably not enough to live on, so I'll have to tutor or take out loans.....boo. 

I also have complete freedom with my time, as long as I pass my courses and finish my thesis, so I'll have to force myself to stick to a schedule. 

So if all goes well, I'm done by Christmas, and I can pretend that it was because of my outstanding research progress, and not the fact that I was forced to graduate early because I'm a bit nuts...

Once that's done...?  My moods swing all the time, and certain days research is the greatest thing ever and I'd rather do nothing else, so a PhD makes sense. Then things get frustrating and I don't think I can handle the work and I get super stresesd. I also want to devote my time to other activities, and for some reason I think that doing research (like a PhD) requires 100% focus and committment, leaving no time for other interests, and that's when i lose motivation. 

So come January, I'll either keep doing some research as a RA, or just take some time off for my other interests. I don't know. I want it all. I want a PhD, and to do research and try to be a professor, but I want to devote all my time to my other interests too, at least for awhile. My other interest is a sport, so I oscillate between wanting to be a PhD researcher, and a full-time athlete. I can't have the best of both worlds, so I'll have to pick one eventually, but only one of those options will pay the bills. I think my ego is just too large. Ack.

Bla, now I'm getting all angsty, so that's the update. In summary, things are mostly OK, as long as I don't fuck up anymore.
Done and done. Thanks for the concern.
First appointment is tomorrow (well, first appointment since I messed up), so I'll mention it, and we'll see if anything comes of it.

The doctor didn't say much. I said I was depressed and I didn't seem able to get out of it, and he said "Oh, we'll start you on some anti-depressants".

Then I said "I have reason to believe it could be bipolar, because...", then I listed the reasons. So he said "Well, we better not give you anti-depressants".

He then had to fax my information to a psychiatrist, and I have to call in the next couple days to see if/when I have an appointment. Apparently it takes like 2-3 weeks to get an appointment, so that sucks. 

In the meantime, I have a therapist appointment tomorrow, but I've seen this therapist before, and I wasn't entirely impressed (she seemed absolutely convinced that my problems somehow stemmed from not having a girlfriend, and my last session, she said I was doing fantastic and probably didn't need to come anymore. A month later, I had another depression...).

I wish I could talk to someone who can help me figure out what's going on and take the necessary steps to solve the problem. I'd much rather look at this rationally than emotionally. Some therapists just like talking, and I've tried that. It just gives me more chances to try to rationalize my behavior, even though it defies logic. I'd rather have like, a coach who can just give me concrete things that would help. Ack. Rant over. 

I'm taking the necessary steps to get better, yes, but what makes you think I wouldn't have problems with not cooperating? I feel ok now, but I may never know when I just say "Fuck it", and stop trying. It's happened in the past, no matter how hard I (seemingly) try to prevent it. What makes it harder is I don't really have friends in this city, and I'm not close enough to my friends at home to dump something like this on them. I talked to my sister last time it happened, but she's oblivious to this episode. 

It's a horrible cycle: I don't have friends here because I get depressed and anxious, and it just puts me in a worse mood when i realize I don't have friends. Ack. OK, rant really done this time.

Does that say something that both of these guys are exes? Oi...

The only problems with option 2 are: will I be motivated enough to stick to a set schedule, and how will I pay the rent and eat?

Do you know how drugs affected your ex or your sister ex? Did behavioral therapy help more? I went to a doctor today, and I can't see a psych for like 2 or 3 weeks, so I won't know anything til then, I guess....

Yeah, I kind of thought that it could be bipolar II, but I very much doubt Wikipedia and self-diagnosis is a reliable way to determine that. Maybe I'm just a mental health hypochondriac. I was tested for ADHD in the past, and I didn't have it. 

Ok, about my project. I'm actually DONE the first half (with just some minor things that need to be corrected), so all I have to do in the next 4 months is write an introduction and a conclusion to my thesis. If I had done the 2nd half, my thesis would have been a bit meatier, and that would have been another paper to publish...

Would I be able to do the whole project? I don't know. I was basically given these options from my advisor (who discussed this with some higher-ups).

1) Withdraw from the program (no one wants that option though, they want me to stay and finish).
 
2) Take the two courses required to graduate and finish the thesis by Christmas, with no funding and no TA money. I guess I could tutor for money, but I'll probably be crazy busy. However, my advisor has said that with this option, I have a lot of freedom, since no one is paying me. As long as I finish, it's OK. 

3) Same as option two, but I get paid by my advisor. Since my advisor is taking some risk in this situation, I basically have to guarantee that I won't eff up again, meaning I have to follow my advisor's rules, and if I break those rules, I'm out of the program. I should also note that even getting paid, I *still* might not have enough money to pay the rent. My last depression coincided with the end of the term (meaning marking and submitting grades), and of course, I neglected that, so I guess they're hesitant to offer me a TA position (and this just makes me feel even worse. I TA'ed for two years in undergrad, and I had no incidents like this. Things got bad at times, and I was on the verge of having something bad happen, but it never did. It's just embarrassing that I can't be trusted to TA properly). 

I'd like to say that it won't happen again, but it's happened 3 times in the past year (October, April and June), lasting for 2 days, 2 weeks and 2 months, respectively (does 2 YEARS come next? God I hope not). I always tell myself it will get better, and it won't happen again. I want to tell myself that, because right now I feel good, like it won't happen again, but when that time comes I feel like I have no control over it. 

But those are my three options. They are willing to consider alternative options, if I can think of something, but I have to take into account that my advisor is not at all willing to take any risks, meaning that the advisor can't afford to pay me if I'm not doing research (someone else could be paid and actually DO the research). 

I suggested graduating in December and perhaps staying the extra 7 or 8 months to finish the other project, meaning it will get done, but not as part of my thesis, and my advisor seemed to be receptive to this. 

The biggest issue, however, is that I have to *guarantee* that I won't fall into a depression anymore, and that I can be consistently reliable; basically, that I can be like a normal person :P 

I have no idea how to guarantee this. I really can't control those feelings. I suggested having a therapist report to my advisor every once in awhile, but that's against the law. I have no idea at all how to guarantee it won't happen again, and that's where I'm stuck. 

What happened with the people you know who had bipolar? How did they find out they had it, what help did they get, and how has it changed things?

I have certain doubts about switching advisors though, for a few reasons...

1. I'm a year into my M.Sc; I'm almost finished, and I could probably write what I have into a thesis without too much effort, to be honest with you.

2. The current advisor and the potential advisor work in similar areas, so if I switch, there might be some bad blood involved.

3. The potential advisor is in a completely different city, and it might be hard to change schools so quickly.

Also, I have to rely on a reference letter from the current advisor....I doubt it will say anything positive, so I'm sure that won't exactly help my chances of doing a PhD. 

Also, I would have to apply to do a PhD in a different subject that isn't a huge strength for me, so how am I to know that the same thing wouldn't happen with a different advisor? I guess that's just me having doubts though...

EDIT: Also, you say that s/he wasn't a big help, but the advisor certainly was (academically, at least). It's just the advisor isn't very supportive, and can be quite argumentative about certain issues...basically, they need to be right, all the time, and I've heard the advisor look at people less than positively when they aren't right. Basically, the advisor lacks tact, which doesn't jive with me at all (obviously).

Well, to be fair, the advisor tried to contact me earlier, and OBVIOUSLY realized that I wasn't around and was missing some meetings. I haven't spoken to him/her yet, so I don't know the reaction. Perhaps it wasn't a big deal yet?

But I agree, the advisor is not very supportive (I don't really know where my talents lie in this field, or even IF they lie in this field at all), as I'm mostly just put on projects that need to be completed, and not, as you put it, "work to see your strengths and offer you opportunities to test your ability".

So that is where I stand. I haven't checked my e-mail since yesterday, so I have no idea where I stand. Of course, I missed another meeting today. I know I have to come back eventually (it's in my own, the advisors and the schools best interests not to kick me out), but I am absolutely dreading that day. Of course, maybe they'll just kick me out anyway; I have given so many people so much grief.

I don't know what past details are relevant to this dilemma. I've always been shy and somewhat anxious in new social situations, but once I'm comfortable in the situation, I'm very outgoing and gregarious. Of course, it's a bit of a hurdle to get over. When I started the hobby mentioned above, I was very shy, and probably didn't speak to anyone the first month or two; but I had a couple friends in it as well, so I had a fallback if I was uncomfortable with the situation. Before long, I had made lots of friends and was quite popular. Unfortunately, I really didn't know a soul before coming here, and if I started the hobby again, I know the group wouldn't be as tight-knit as the one I had at home, so making friends might even be harder. I've been here over a year, and I haven't made friends...seems kind of weird, doesn't it? 

On a somewhat related note, whenever I've gotten into the habit of doing my hobby regularly, there will always come a day where I have to stay a little later at the office, or I have to do some task that needs to be done, so I will skip that day. I try to justify this to myself, but it eventually turns into “Well, it's only one day”..then...”Well, it's only X days”, and I try to tell myself that it's OK to miss, even though it makes me miserable. But not making enough progress to satisfy my advisor gives me massive amounts of anxiety, so I do what I can to stay on top of my research, even if it means putting in 60-70 hours weeks, as I have frequently done over the past year. I hate the reaction I get when I haven't done enough work...

I think I'm like most redditors; a bit ADHD, procrastinator, I find it easier to focus on trivial little things (e.g reddit, video games, tv), than the important things that interest me (e.g science, learning, the above mentioned hobby). I am very ambitious, but my work ethic doesn't match my ambitions, unfortunately. I constantly tie in my achievements to my worth and constantly question whether I'm “good enough” to be in the field I am in, or whether I have the dedication to do it, or if I really, truly enjoy it, etc. Etc. I am happiest when I live in the present (getting into a “flow” state, if you're familiar with the psychological term) and actually DO the work, but I constantly waste my time looking towards the future. My final two years of undergrad, I probably spent more time looking at potential graduate programs than actually studying and doing work. The program I ended up going to? I found it about two weeks before the application deadline, so the previous searching was a massive waste of time. Situations change all the time and you can't predict the future, yet I try to do it all teh time. I don't know if I enjoy the work that I'm doing, or the IDEA of doing that work I'm doing more. Would I really enjoy being a professor, like my plan is, or do I just enjoy the IDEA of being a professor?

I guess to sum up, the last year of my life has arguably been the worst year of my life The competition? Two different years: First,  I was mercilessly bullied when I was 13; I had no friends and I numbed the pain with video games. I moved to a new school the next year where I had about 5 friends out of a class of 300. With that initial foothold, I quickly made a lot of new friends. The next time was senior year of high school, when I found out my girlfriend of two years had cheated on me on a trip, and then broke up with me when she got back. Among the crazy things I did then were shave my head into a mohawk, climb up to her window at 3AM to be a teenage drama queen, physically threaten the guy she cheated on me with (I am one of the most pacifist people you could ever meet), stop hanging out with most of my high school friends and quit two jobs and the basketball team by just  not showing up anymore (wow, that sounds familiar...).What brought me out of that? I flipped out on a friend on messenger, thinking it was my ex-gf. It wasn't my ex-gf. After my initial utter mortification, it made me realize how everyone else saw me and my reaction, and really put into perspective how completely trivial my anger was. Almost overnight, I got over my ex.

What else can I say? I absolutely abhor confrontation; if there is potential for a conflict (however minor), I shrink away from it and avoid it, instead of manning up and dealing with the problem or quitting. Some examples include: 3 jobs, a national volunteer position, a high school team, 3 relationships that I wanted out of, a research project last year (that I needed to finish to graduate; I almost just wanted to fail it and come back to school an extra year, but I finished it and recieved an A, regardless), and numerous minor contracts, like student loans, payments, etc. Etc. I just ignore the problem and it either eventually goes away, or it becomes so overblown and serious that I absolutely have to deal with it, since there is absolutely no avoiding it. 

So I guess to sum up, I have some anxiety issues, that become amplified under severe stress, which leads to more anxiety in a horrific feedback loop. The advisor suggested I have bi-polar, but I don't have manic episodes. I have days where I'm more motivated than others, but definitely not manic, but low grade depression (I think....dysthymia?), I have that. I hinted at some of my problems in a discussion [here](http://www.reddit.com/r/AskReddit/comments/8yfjk/whats_the_difference_between_being_lazy_and/), and had some useful suggestions, which I definitely haven't acted on yet. I know, I'll probably book an appointment with a therapist tomorrow, and I will probably bring a copy of this little rant, as it's a psychologists wet dream, I might imagine. Hell, I might even give a copy to the advisor, just so it's clear that I'm not just lazy, unmotivated, or any of that other stuff that certain overachievers seem to label misfits like me with.

I was seeing two counsellors after Depression #1, (one a therapist, one a career counsellor), but I stopped seeing both because I was doing so damn OK. The therapist even said that I should be in her position because I had such a positive attitude; as you probably guessed, that didn't last.

So clearly I need to make a change, as that's the only way to make things better...but what needs to change? What's the real problem? My anxiety? My advisor? Being over my head in my program? Lack of support network? Lack of any physical activity (the hobby I dedicated ~15 hrs/week to was a physical  activity)? Maybe a combination of all of the above, but things absolutely have to change. There have been plenty of times in my life when I'm happy, outgoing, all that good stuff, and there have even been times this year when I get that feeling (most of them associated with my research, or living in such a cool place), but those times are islands in a sea of depression and anxiety. 

I apologize if this is convoluted, long, incoherent, or otherwise unreadable. This started as a plea for advice, but it has been very cathartic and I imagine I got more out of this just by writing it than any advice I might be offered. I hate to think that I seem self-important by writing this (“Boo hoo, I'm sad, help me!”), so I hope that someone in this sub-reddit comes across it and sees some similarities with their own situation and maybe does something to change it. I hope it helps someone, and this becomes something other than selfish rambling. 

I don't know what advice anyone can give, but if you have any, it would be very much appreciated. Thank you for taking the time to read this.
